item.title: NPP Lecture 1 Review: Intro to Computer Science & Floating-Point Arithmetic
item.description:
NPP Lecture 1 Review: Intro to Computer Science & Floating-Point Arithmetic

Topics: Python basics · standard library · algorithm complexity · computer fundamentals · binary · IEEE-754 floating point

Part 1: Intro to Computer Science (morning)

1. Why Python?

  • An interpreted, general-purpose programming language; popular and in high demand.
  • Competes with R in the data-science space and has a huge ML/deep-learning ecosystem.
  • "Easy to do simple things, not too hard to do complex things, possible to do really complex things."

2. Hello World and the command line

print("Hello World!")
  • Save it as a .py file and run it in a terminal with python scripts/hello_world.py.
  • In Jupyter/IPython, ! runs a shell command and % runs a magic command; neither may be used in a plain Python (.py) file.

3. The powerful standard library

The import statement is Python's most powerful operation; the standard library ships with every install:

Category Module Purpose
Text processing re Regular expressions
Text processing string Common string operations
Data types copy Shallow/deep copy
Data types collections Containers (defaultdict, namedtuple, …)
Data types datetime Dates and times
Numeric/math math Mathematical functions
Numeric/math random Pseudo-random numbers
Numeric/math decimal Decimal fixed/floating-point arithmetic
Numeric/math fractions Rational numbers
Numeric/math statistics Statistical functions
Functional itertools Efficient looping iterators
Functional functools Higher-order functions
Functional operator Operators as functions
Files/dirs os / glob / shutil / tempfile OS interfaces / path matching / high-level file ops
Persistence pickle Object serialization (save to disk)
Persistence sqlite3 SQLite DB interface
File formats csv / json CSV / JSON read-write
System services sys / argparse / time System params / CLI parsing / time
Net/GUI urllib / http / tkinter URL handling / HTTP / basic GUI

re quick reference

import re
re.findall(pattern, text)   # all matches
re.search(pattern, text)    # search anywhere (first match)
re.match(pattern, text)     # match from the start
  • . matches any non-newline character; * matches 0+ of the previous; \w matches word characters.

collections examples

from collections import defaultdict, namedtuple

d = defaultdict(lambda: "not set!")
d["James"]          # -> "not set!"

Pets = namedtuple("Pets", ["cat", "dog"])
p = Pets("Tiddles", dog="Rover")
p.dog               # -> "Rover"

math and numpy don't always mix

import math, numpy as np
math.sin(np.pi/6)      # OK — Python understands numpy scalars
arr = np.array([0, np.pi/6, np.pi/2])
np.sin(arr)            # OK — vectorized
math.sin(arr)          # ERROR — Python doesn't understand numpy arrays

4. Good-code principles (acronyms)

Acronym Expansion Meaning
DRY Don't Repeat Yourself Avoid duplication
SOC Separation of Concerns Keep concerns separate
KISS Keep It Simple, Stupid Stay simple
YAGNI You Ain't Gonna Need It Don't over-engineer

5. Time/space complexity (Big O)

Think of a computer as a Turing machine: every algorithm is a trade-off between space (memory) and time (runtime).

  • my_max(x): one pass to find the max → grows linearly, $\mathcal{O}(n)$.
  • find_duplicates(x): nested loops → grows quadratically, $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$.
  • permute(x): generate all permutations → time and output space grow factorial, $\mathcal{O}(n!)$.

Use %timeit (Jupyter magic) to measure runtime and a log-log plot to read off the order.

6. Computer architecture and the storage hierarchy

  • Low level: doped silicon wafers form transistors in logic circuits.
  • Storage layers (faster/more expensive at the top): CPU registers → CPU cache → RAM → disk.
  • Moving data between layers costs time → computers are faster on "nearby" data.
  • All modern computers are binary: high voltage = "on", low voltage = "off".

7. Binary and integer representation

Positive integers

$2381$ expands by place value; binary $1001_2 = 1\cdot8+0\cdot4+0\cdot2+1\cdot1 = 9_{10}$.

int("1001", base=2)   # 9
bin(9)                # '0b1001'
bin(int(3.5))         # 3  -> can't do bin(3.5)

Two storage schemes:

  1. Store "how many bits + the number itself" → Python uses this, giving arbitrary-precision integers (bounded by memory).
  2. Fixed bit count with leading zeros → NumPy uses this (efficient, interoperable with C).

Integer overflow

Fixed-width integers overflow. An 8-bit unsigned 11111111 (255) + 1 wraps to 0:

import numpy as np
x = np.array([int("11111111", 2)], dtype=np.uint8)   # 255
(x + 1)[0]   # -> 0 (overflow wraparound)

Negative integers: two's complement

  • Option 1 (sign bit): steal the top bit for the sign — needs separate add/subtract circuitry, complicated.
  • Option 2 (two's complement): the top bit carries weight $-2^{n-1}$. In 4 bits, $-3 = 1101_2$ ($-8+4+1=-3$).
    • Addition works the same as unsigned: $-3+3 = 1101+0011 = 0000 = 0$.
    • Negate by flipping all bits and adding 1: $-3=1101 \to 0010+1=0011=3$.
np.binary_repr(3, width=4)    # '0011'
np.binary_repr(-3, width=4)   # '1101'

8. Characters and text encoding

  • Computers store only binary, so characters must be encoded as numbers.
  • The most famous encoding is ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange).
  • Python 3 defaults to Unicode (utf-8), covering nearly every world language.
  • Text is stored as a sequence of code points, plus its length/end position.

Part 2: Floating-point arithmetic (afternoon)

The core mystery: why is $0.1 + 0.2 \ne 0.3$?

9. The IEEE-754 standard

Established in 1985 by the IEEE to fix inconsistencies between manufacturers (previously $a+b$ differed across machines).

Any non-zero real $x$ can be written in normalised binary scientific notation:

$$x = (-1)^{s} \times (1.f)_{2} \times 2^{e-\text{bias}}$$

  • sign $s$: 1 bit.
  • exponent $e$: 8 bits (single) or 11 bits (double) — stored with a bias added.
  • mantissa (significand) $f$: 23 bits (single) or 52 bits (double); the leading 1 is implicit (not stored), so precision is one bit more.
Precision Total bits Sign Exponent Mantissa
single (float32) 32 1 8 23
double (float64) 64 1 11 52
quadruple 128 1 15 112

Don't memorise — query np.finfo().

Single precision (32-bit)

$$x = (-1)^s \times (1.f)_2 \times 2^{e-127}$$

  • Exponent $e$: $0 < e < 255$; $e=0$ is reserved for $\pm0$ and subnormals, $e=255$ for $\pm\infty$ and NaN. Bias = 127, so the true exponent ranges $2^{-126}$ to $2^{127}$.
  • Mantissa $m=1.f$: $1 \le m \le 2 - 2^{-23}$.
  • Largest number $\approx (2-2^{-23})\cdot 2^{127} \approx 2^{128} \approx 3.4\times10^{38}$.
  • Smallest positive normal $= 2^{-126} \approx 1.18\times10^{-38}$; subnormals reach $2^{-149}\approx1.4\times10^{-45}$ (at the cost of precision).

Double precision (64-bit)

$$x = (-1)^s \times (1.f)_2 \times 2^{e-1023}$$

  • 11-bit exponent, bias = 1023; 52-bit mantissa.
  • Largest $\approx 2^{1024} \approx 1.8\times10^{308}$; smallest positive normal $\approx 2^{-1022}\approx2.2\times10^{-308}$; subnormals to $2^{-1074}\approx4.9\times10^{-324}$.

Machine epsilon ε

  • Machine numbers: the finite set of exactly representable reals; the machine number for $x$ is $\mathrm{fl}(x)$.
  • Machine ε: the distance between $1$ and the next larger machine number.
    • Single: $\epsilon = 2^{-23} \approx 1.19\times10^{-7}$.
    • Double: $\epsilon = 2^{-52} \approx 2.22\times10^{-16}$.
  • Because we round to the nearest machine number, $\mathrm{fl}(1+x)\ne1$ as soon as $x > \epsilon/2$.

Precision and resolution

  • Single: 23 mantissa bits → $\log_{10}(2^{23})\approx6.9$, i.e. 6 reliable significant digits, resolution $10^{-6}$.
  • Double: 52 mantissa bits → $\log_{10}(2^{52})\approx15.65$, i.e. 15 reliable significant digits, resolution $10^{-15}$.
import numpy as np
f = np.finfo(np.float64)
print(f.bits, f.nmant, f.nexp)   # total / mantissa / exponent bits
print(f.max, f.tiny, f.eps)      # largest / smallest normal / machine epsilon
print(f.precision, f.resolution)

10. Rounding, overflow and underflow

  • Every operation rounds: $\mathrm{fl}(\mathrm{fl}(a)+\mathrm{fl}(b))$.
  • Underflow: numbers below the smallest normal first lose precision (subnormals) and eventually round to zero.
  • Overflow: IEEE-754 default is $\pm\infty$ (e.g. 1e308 * 10 → inf); some operations raise OverflowError (e.g. 2.0**10000, math.exp(1000)).

11. The five "surprises" — must understand

Surprise 1: $1 + x \ne 1$ does not hold

x = 1e-16
print(1 + x != 1)   # False

Reason: $x=10^{-16} < \epsilon/2\approx1.11\times10^{-16}$, so $1+x$ rounds back to machine number $1$. With $x=2\times10^{-16}$ ($>\epsilon/2$ but $<\epsilon$), 1 + x != 1 is True.

Surprise 2: $0.1+0.2\ne0.3$

print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)   # False

Reason: a finite decimal may not be finite in binary. $(0.1)_{10}=(0.0001100110011\ldots)_2$, like $0.3333\ldots$ in decimal. fl(0.1)+fl(0.2) rounds to something other than fl(0.3).

Surprise 3: associativity fails

a, b, c = 1e16, -1e16, 1.0
print((a+b)+c == a+(b+c))   # False

Reason: every operation rounds. $(a+b)+c = 0+1 = 1$, but $a+(b+c)=1e16+(-1e16)$; $b+c$ rounds back to $-1e16$, giving 0. Machine numbers are not evenly spaced (sparser for larger magnitudes).

Surprise 4: catastrophic cancellation

a, b = 1.0000001, 1.0000000
print(a - b == 1e-7)   # False

Reason: subtracting two nearly-equal numbers. $\mathrm{fl}(1.0000001)$ carries a tiny rounding error; the subtraction itself is exact (Sterbenz lemma), but the leading 1.000000 cancels, so the absolute error stays while the result shrinks $10^7\times$ — the relative error is amplified about $10^7\times$. In general:

$$\text{relative error}\lesssim\frac{|a|+|b|}{|a-b|}\cdot\frac{\epsilon}{2}$$

  • Subtraction doesn't create error — it exposes the rounding errors already in $a,b$; the closer they are, the worse the amplification.
  • Remedy: rewrite formulas to avoid subtracting nearly-equal numbers, e.g. $\sqrt{x+1}-\sqrt{x}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x+1}+\sqrt{x}}$.

Surprise 5: accumulated error

a, b = 100, 0.1
s = 0
for _ in range(a):
    s += b
print(a * b == s)   # False

Reason: the error in fl(0.1) accumulates over 100 iterations.

12. Take-home message

Never compare floats with ==! Use

$$|a-b|<\text{tol}$$

or simply:

np.isclose(0.1+0.2, 0.3, atol=1e-15, rtol=1e-5)

13. Companion exercises

  1. dec2bin: integer part — repeated division by 2 (remainders reversed); fractional part — repeated multiplication by 2 (take the integer part), capped at max_fractional_digits (52) to avoid infinite loops.
  2. Counting machine numbers: use itertools.product to enumerate all bit combinations, then deduplicate and count.
  3. IEEE-754 encode/decode: convert a decimal to its 32/64-bit string, or a bit string back to decimal (sign + exponent + mantissa concatenation).

item.title: NPP Lecture 2 Review: NumPy & Pandas
item.description:
NPP Lecture 2 Review: NumPy & Pandas

Topics: NumPy arrays · vectorised operations · broadcasting · Pandas Series/DataFrame · data cleaning · groupby · merging · time series

Part 1: NumPy

1. Import conventions and pitfalls

import numpy as np            # conventional alias
from numpy import *           # ❌ dangerous — overwrites builtins like sum/max

2. Core concept: ndarray

  • NumPy's fundamental object.
  • list vs array: a list stores pointers to objects, an array stores values contiguously — arrays are faster and use less memory.
  • Don't use the built-in array module: only 1-D and inflexible types.

3. Creating arrays

Method Example Notes
np.array np.array([1,2,3]); np.array([[1,2],[3,4]]) from lists; same-depth lengths must match
np.zeros np.zeros(3); np.zeros((3,3)) all zeros
np.ones np.ones((3,3)) all ones
np.full np.full(shape, value) fill a value
np.arange np.arange(start, stop, step) excludes stop
np.linspace np.linspace(0,10,6) fixed count, includes stop
np.eye np.eye(3) identity matrix

4. Array attributes

a = np.eye(3)
a.ndim      # 2      number of dimensions
a.shape     # (3,3)  size of each dimension
a.size      # 9      = np.prod(shape)
a.nbytes    # 72     = 9 × 8 bytes
a.dtype     # float64

5. Shape manipulation

  • .reshape(4,3) / .reshape(3,-1): change shape, size unchanged; -1 is inferred and may appear only once.
  • .ravel() / .flatten(): flatten to 1-D (order="K" follows memory order).
  • .T: transpose.
  • 1-D vectors: np.matmul(a,b) and np.matmul(b,a) may differ (row/column not strictly distinguished).

6. Types (dtype)

  • Inferred: [1,2.5,3] → float; [1,2,"Hi"] → str.
  • Explicit: np.array([...], dtype=np.int32).
  • Pitfall: int_arr[1] = 3.5 silently truncates to an integer (no error).

7. Operations and broadcasting

  • Element-wise operators + - * / ** % (map to np.add/subtract/multiply/divide/power/mod).
  • Matrix multiplication: @ / np.matmul / np.dot.
  • Broadcasting: arrays of different shapes can operate; the smaller is broadcast to the larger (at least one dimension compatible).

8. Indexing and slicing

  • Multi-dim index arr[0,0]; multi-dim slice arr[1:3,1:6:2] (== arr[slice(1,3), slice(1,6,2)]).
  • Slice assignment arr[1:3,1:3]=0 follows broadcasting.
  • ⚠️ View pitfall: new = old[1:3,1:3] is a view — mutating new mutates old; use .copy() to avoid.
  • Boolean indexing: arr[arr>5]; arr[arr%3==0]=-1.

9. Linear algebra (np.linalg)

Method Purpose
np.linalg.det(A) determinant
np.linalg.eig(A) eigenvalues/vectors
np.linalg.norm(A) norm
np.linalg.inv(A) matrix inverse (direct method)
np.linalg.solve(A,b) solve linear system (prefer to inv)

10. Record arrays (prelude to Pandas)

arr = np.rec.array(...)
arr["val_1"]        # access a field by name
arr.val_2[1]

Part 2: Pandas

11. Import and Series

import pandas as pd
  • Series: a 1-D labelled array — like a NumPy array but indexed by labels; behaves like a fast dict.
  • Create: pd.Series(data=list) / pd.Series(data, index=labels, name="...") / pd.Series(arr) / pd.Series(dic) (keys become the index).
  • Select by label ser["first name"].
  • ⚠️ Operations align on the index: ser1 + ser2 aligns by label, not position.

12. DataFrame

  • A 2-D table (like a spreadsheet): rows = records/index, columns = fields.
  • Create: pd.DataFrame(data, index=[...], columns=[...]) or a dict {"col":[values...]}.

13. Reading and writing

Method Example Notes
pd.read_csv pd.read_csv("df1.csv") 30+ parameters
index column pd.read_csv(..., index_col=0) use an existing column as index
to_csv df.to_csv("example", index=False) write back
pd.read_excel/to_excel read_excel("f.xlsx", sheet_name="Sheet1") data only, no formulas/charts

14. Selection

  • .columns / .index: column names / index.
  • Single column df["Y"] (returns a Series); multiple columns df[["Y","Z"]].
  • SQL-style df.Y: discouraged, has limitations.
  • .iloc (position): df.iloc[0,:], df.iloc[:,0], df.iloc[[1,2],0] (.at is similar).
  • .loc (label): df.loc["A"], df.loc["B","Y"], df.loc[["A","B"],["Z","Y"]].
  • Order: loc/iloc put rows before columns (same as NumPy, opposite of Python lists).

15. Add/remove

  • New column df["new"] = df["Z"] + df["Y"] (a column is just a Series).
  • Remove df.drop("new", axis=1) / df.drop("A", axis=0): not in-place by default — pass inplace=True.
  • del df["col"]: in-place delete.

16. Conditional filtering

  • df[df>0], df[df["Z"]>0], df[(df["X"]>0)&(df["Y"]>1)] (df>0 is a boolean DataFrame).
  • Combine with & (and), | (or); each condition must be parenthesised.
  • .isin (membership), .isnull/.notnull (null checks).

17. Index operations

  • reset_index(): back to 0,1,2…; set_index("col"): not in-place by default.
  • MultiIndex: pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays([[...],[...]]); select by level mdf.loc["Player 1", :], mdf.xs("Test 1", level=1) (levels start at 0).

18. Common operations and statistics

  • .head(): peek at the first rows.
  • .unique() / .nunique(): unique values / count of unique values.
  • .value_counts(): occurrence counts.
  • .duplicated() / .drop_duplicates(inplace=True): find/drop duplicate rows.
  • Statistics: .mean() .std() .median() .sum() .max() .min() (watch numeric_only=True).
  • .describe(): summary (can .transpose()).

19. map and apply

  • .map: df["col1"].map(lambda p: p - mean) — element-wise, not in-place.
  • .apply: df["col1"].apply(f, n=4) or args=[4] for extra args; can use builtins like len.

20. Types and missing values

  • .dtype / .dtypes: one column / all columns.
  • .astype("float64"): converts (not a forced cast).
  • Types: float64 / int64 / object (strings are stored as object).
  • NaN: missing values are NaN, always float64.
  • Check: df.isnull() / df.notnull().
  • ⚠️ Effect on math: df.sum() skips NaN by default; df.sum(skipna=False) propagates NaN.
  • dropna(): drop by row/column/threshold (axis=1, thresh=2).
  • fillna(value="FILL") / df["A"].fillna(df["A"].mean()): fill.
  • replace: swap "Unknown" etc. for np.nan.

21. Grouping and pivoting

  • df.groupby("Course"): returns a GroupBy object.
  • .groups / .get_group("NPP"): inspect groups / fetch one group.
  • Aggregations: .mean() .std() .max() .min() .count() .describe().
  • .agg: df.groupby(["Course"]).agg([len,"min","max"]) custom aggregation.
  • pivot_table(values, index, columns, aggfunc, fill_value): reshape + aggregate; aggfunc can be a function/list/dict.

22. Combining

  • pd.concat([df1,df2,df3]): glue; vertical by default (axis=0), horizontal with axis=1.
  • pd.merge(left,right,how="inner",on="key"): SQL-JOIN-like.
    • how: inner (intersection) / outer (union) / left / right.
    • multi-key on=["key1","key2"].
  • .join: left.join(right) merges columns on the index; how="outer".

23. Visualisation

  • .plot.hist(): histogram.
  • .plot.scatter("A","B"): scatter plot.

24. Time series

  • Parse dates: pd.read_csv("Tide.csv", index_col="Date", parse_dates=True, dayfirst=True).
  • .sample(n=5): random sample.
  • Date parts: df.index.day / .month / .date.
  • .resample("D").mean() / df["Hs"].resample("ME").max(): aggregate by date, can fill gaps.
  • .asfreq("ME"): take points at a frequency without aggregating.
  • pd.to_datetime(dates, format="mixed", dayfirst=True, utc=True): build a DatetimeIndex.
  • Date ambiguity: numeric dates must consistently be DD/MM/YYYY or MM/DD/YYYY.

Quick-reference table (≈40 NumPy + ≈60 Pandas items)

| Area | Method / concept | Example | Key point | |---|---|---|---| | NumPy·create | np.array / np.zeros / np.ones / np.full | np.full(shape, value) | build arrays | | NumPy·create | np.arange / np.linspace / np.eye | np.arange(start, stop, step) | arange excludes, linspace includes the stop | | NumPy·attrs | .ndim / .shape / .size / .nbytes / .dtype | (3,3); 9; 72 | dims / shape / count / bytes / type | | NumPy·shape | .reshape / .ravel / .flatten / .T | arr.reshape(3,-1) | -1 at most once | | NumPy·ops | elementwise + - * / ** %; matmul @/np.matmul/np.dot | — | broadcasting | | NumPy·index | multi-dim index/slice/boolean | arr[arr>5] | slices are views — use .copy() | | NumPy·linalg | det / eig / norm / inv / solve | np.linalg.solve(A,b) | prefer solve to inv | | Pandas·Series | create / label select / index-aligned ops | ser1 + ser2 | aligns by index label | | Pandas·DataFrame | create / IO / select | df[["Y","Z"]] | rows = records, columns = fields | | Pandas·select | .iloc (position) / .loc (label) | df.loc["B","Y"] | rows first, columns second | | Pandas·add/del | new column / drop / del | df.drop("new", axis=1) | drop not in-place | | Pandas·cond | filter / & / | / .isin / .isnull | df[(df["X"]>0)&(df["Y"]>1)] | parenthesise each condition | | Pandas·index | reset_index / set_index / MultiIndex / .xs | mdf.xs("Test 1", level=1) | levels from 0 | | Pandas·ops | .head / .unique / .value_counts / .drop_duplicates / .describe | — | data exploration | | Pandas·map/apply | .map / .apply | df["col"].apply(f, n=4) | not in-place | | Pandas·types | .astype / float64/int64/object | — | strings stored as object | | Pandas·missing | isnull / dropna / fillna / replace | df.sum(skipna=False) | sum skips NaN by default | | Pandas·group | groupby / .agg / pivot_table | df.groupby("Course").agg([len,"min","max"]) | aggregation | | Pandas·combine | concat / merge / join | pd.merge(l,r,how="inner",on="key") | inner/outer/left/right | | Pandas·time | parse_dates / resample / asfreq / to_datetime | df.resample("D").mean() | date aggregation |

Common pitfalls ⚠️

  1. np.arange excludes the stop; np.linspace includes it.
  2. NumPy slices are views (mutating them changes the original); Pandas drop/set_index/map are not in-place by default.
  3. Pandas multi-condition filters must be parenthesised and use &/| (not and/or).
  4. Series arithmetic aligns on the index label, not position.
  5. df.sum() skips NaN by default; pass skipna=False to propagate.
  6. Assigning a float into an integer array silently truncates.

item.title: NPP Lecture 3 Review: Debugging
item.description:
NPP Lecture 3 Review: Debugging

Topics: exceptions & tracebacks · avoiding bugs · static analysis · minimum failing examples · manual debugging · the pdb debugger · AI-assisted debugging

1. Why debugging matters

  • Developers often spend as much (or more) time debugging as writing "real" code.
  • Debugging is a skill you must actively develop to stay productive.

Famous bugs in history

Event Notes
The first "bug" (1947) Grace Hopper logged an actual moth stuck in a relay, popularising the term "debugging"
Y2K Two-digit years caused the year-2000 problem; billions spent fixing it worldwide
Dhahran missile (1991) A Patriot system clock drifted ⅓ s over 100 h, causing a failed intercept that killed 28 US soldiers

Fun bug types

Type Characteristic
Heisenbug Disappears or changes when you try to observe/debug it (quantum "observer effect")
Bohrbug Reproduces reliably under well-defined (possibly unknown) conditions
Mandelbug So complex it's practically unfixable (after Mandelbrot)
Schroedinbug Only manifests once you realise it "shouldn't work at all"

2. Python tracebacks and exceptions

Reading a traceback

A traceback is the call-stack report produced when an exception is raised. Read it bottom-to-top (the last line is where the exception fired, not necessarily the bug's root cause).

NameError: name 'exp' is not defined
  • The first line is the exception type; below Traceback (most recent call last) each call is listed.

Common exceptions (be able to trigger each)

Exception How to trigger
ImportError from numpy import alalalala
ModuleNotFoundError import what
ZeroDivisionError 1 / 0
IndexError [1,2,3][100]
TypeError "hello" + None
SyntaxError syntax errors (e.g. 2+2 =="4")
IndentationError missing indentation under for
RecursionError def f(): return f()

You can define custom exceptions; see the Python docs.

3. Avoiding bugs (write with debugging in mind)

  • Everyone writes buggy code — write it to be testable and debuggable.
  • KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid): what's the simplest thing that could work?
  • DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself): each piece of knowledge has a single authoritative representation.
  • Loose coupling: limit interdependencies between parts of the code.
  • Meaningful names: name variables/functions/modules clearly, not cryptically.

4. Static analysis

  • Interpreted (Python/Matlab/JS) vs compiled (C/C++/Fortran): compiled languages catch some bugs at compile time; Python misses that step.
  • Python static-analysis tools:
    • pyflakes: simplest and fast; catches syntax errors, missing imports, name typos.
    • flake8: pyflakes + pep8, also flags PEP8 style violations.
    • pylint, pychecker; notebook version flake8-nb.
  • Integrate into your editor/IDE for big productivity gains.

5. The debugging workflow

No silver bullet, but a strategy helps. Ideal: isolate the bug to a few lines with a short modify-run-fail cycle.

  1. Make it fail reliably — find a test case that fails the same way every time.
  2. Divide and conquer — isolate the module → function → line.
  3. Isolate a minimum failing example (MFE).
  4. Change one thing at a time, re-run the failing case.
  5. Use the debugger to understand what's wrong.
  6. Take notes and be patient.
  7. After fixing, add the case to your test suite to prevent regression.

6. Minimum failing example (MFE)

  • The simplest code that reproduces a bug.
  • Providing an MFE is good practice when asking for help — it drastically cuts debugging time.
  • Open-source maintainers often reply "please provide an MFE".
  • Example: hundreds of lines of Devito code condensed to ~15 lines, then fixed in under an hour.

7. Manual debugging

  • print statements: print values near the suspected line to localise the bug.
x = some_function(inputs)
print(x.property1, x.property2)
  • IPython.embed(): drop into an interactive interpreter mid-code to inspect state.
x = some_function(inputs)
from IPython import embed; embed()

8. The Python debugger (pdb)

What it can do

  • View source; walk up/down the call stack; inspect/modify variable values; set breakpoints.

Three ways to launch

  1. Postmortem (IPython only): after an error, run %debug.
  2. Command line: python -m pdb script.py.
  3. In code: insert breakpoint() where you want to drop in (older equivalent: import pdb; pdb.set_trace()).

Common commands

Command Description
l(list) list code around the current position
p(print) print a variable (p a)
n(ext) next line (doesn't step into functions)
s(tep) next statement (steps into functions)
c(ontinue) continue to the next breakpoint
b(reak) set a breakpoint (b 34)
u(p) / d(own) move up/down the call stack
bt print the call stack
a print local variables
!command run a Python command (vs a pdb command)
q quit
h / help help

Turning warnings into exceptions

np.seterr(all='raise')   # make divide/invalid/over raise, enabling post-mortem debugging

Debugging in pytest

  • pytest --pdb my_test.py: post-mortem on exceptions.
  • pytest --pdb-failure: inspect test failures with the debugger.

GUI/alternative tools

  • pudb (semi-graphical console debugger), VS Code's debug mode, the Mu editor.

9. AI and debugging

  • AI (Copilot, Claude, …) is a powerful assistant but has limits: it can be misled, hallucinate, and write its own bugs.
  • Experience-based tips:
    • Some of the hardest-to-find bugs come from AI-generated code checked too hastily.
    • You are ultimately responsible for all the code you produce.
    • Context matters: chat UIs suit small snippets; agentic tools (Claude Code/Codex) suit large codebases but are often not permitted for assessed work.
  • Learning advice: you must be able to write code from scratch yourself; AI helps with learning (clarifying concepts, suggesting efficient approaches) but relying on it to write/debug code won't benefit you long-term.

10. Summary

  • Everyone writes bugs.
  • Debugging tools save time and energy.
  • Static analysis avoids many simple bugs.
  • Use IPython.embed() for manual debugging.
  • Learn the basics of pdb.

item.title: NPP Lecture 4 Review: Python Data Structures & Classes (OOP and Deep Learning)
item.description:
NPP Lecture 4 Review: Python Data Structures & Classes (OOP and Deep Learning)

Topics: built-in data structures · mutability · standard-library containers · classes & inheritance · magic methods · PyTorch nn.Module

Part 1: Core data structures

1. Objects and name binding

  • Every Python datum is an "object".
  • Python uses duck typing: functions accept any object (unlike C/Java).
  • = binds an object to a name.
x = 7
y = x          # y and x point to the same object
a = list([1,2,3,4])
b = a          # b and a point to the same list (shallow binding!)

2. Mutable vs immutable

Type Mutability
int / float / str / complex / tuple / frozenset immutable
list / set / dict mutable
  • "Updating" an immutable object actually creates a new object — verify with id().
x = 3
print(id(x)); x += 5; print(id(x))   # id changes → new object
  • Small-integer cache: Python caches the integers −5 to 256.
x = 3; y = 3
print(x is y)          # True (same cached object)
a = 12345; b = 12345
print(a is b)          # False
  • Python integers are arbitrary precision, bounded only by memory (sys.getsizeof()).

3. Lists

  • Create with [] or list(): [1,3,5], list((3,4,5)), [_ for _ in range(6,10)].
  • Properties: mutable, one-dimensional (single index), ordered; a collection of other objects; supports iteration.
  • Fast: look up / change elements, append/remove the last element.
  • Slow: add/remove elements other than the last (cost scales with length — the whole block shifts).
  • Implementation: CPython lists are a block of memory addresses; spare space is preallocated, and a full list must be copied wholesale.

List comprehensions

  • [_ for _ in range(6, 10)] is usually the fastest way to build a list (20–25% faster than a for+append loop); prefer it while it stays readable.

4. Tuples

  • Create with commas (usually ()) or tuple(): 1,3,5, (2,3,4), tuple([3,4,5]).
  • Properties: immutable, one-dimensional, ordered — the immutable equivalent of a list.
  • Fast at lookup; slightly less memory than a list (block sized exactly, no spare room).
  • Use a tuple when something should never change.
  • Unpacking: a, b, c = 1, 2, 3 — often used to collect multiple return values.

5. Generators

  • There is no "tuple comprehension"; (x**2 for x in range(3)) is a generator.
  • A generator can be iterated only once; it doesn't store its contents but yields values on demand and discards them — memory-efficient.
  • Easy to trip over:
gen = (x for x in range(4))
print(list(gen))   # [0, 1, 2, 3]
print(list(gen))   # [] (already exhausted!)

6. Sets and frozensets

  • Create with {} or set(): {1,3,5}, set([3,4,5]).
  • Properties: unordered, mutable, a collection of distinct objects.
  • x in S is very fast (orders of magnitude faster than a list).
  • Implementation: a hash table — a large (mostly empty) block plus a hash function mapping values to slots 0..N−1.
    • Add: hash the value → insert at that slot.
    • Lookup: hash the value → check that slot.
    • Collisions (two values hashing to the same slot) are resolved by probing a predictable pattern until the target or an empty slot is found → sets must stay sparse, using more memory than lists.
  • frozenset: the immutable version of a set.

7. Dictionaries (dict)

  • Map keys → values: {"a":1,"b":10}, dict(x=1,y=2), {x:x**2 for x in range(10)}.
  • Like sets, optimized for x in D (fast key lookup).
  • Keys must be immutable and hashable (no lists as keys).
  • Implementation: a hash table like a set, but:
    • a dict stores both the key and (the address of) the value object;
    • a dict preserves insertion order (Python 3.7+), a set does not.
  • Dict comprehensions build dicts quickly, but aren't always faster than a loop (e.g. reversing a dict is about equal).

8. Choosing a data structure

  • Ordered + mutable + indexable → list; fixed → tuple.
  • Deduplication / fast in tests → set; fixed → frozenset.
  • key→value mapping / fast key lookup → dict.
  • Memory-efficient, iterate once → generator.

Part 2: Standard-library extension types

9. The array module

  • Stores a homogeneous collection (one type), more memory-efficient than a list (values, not pointers).
  • But awkward to use; most people ignore it — prefer NumPy.
import array
a = [1,2,3,4,5]
b = array.array('b', a)   # more compact

10. The collections module

Type Notes
namedtuple tuple-like with named fields
deque list-like, fast append/pop at both ends
OrderedDict insertion-ordered dict (now redundant since dicts are ordered; still in legacy code)
defaultdict auto-provides a default value for missing keys via a factory, e.g. defaultdict(int)

Part 3: NumPy / Pandas recap

  • numpy.ndarray: multidimensional arrays (1-D to 64-D); all elements must share one type; if no dtype is given, NumPy picks one that fits the input.
np.array([0,1,2])       # int64
np.array([0,1,2.5])     # float64
np.array([0,'hat',sum]) # object
  • pandas.Series: a labelled 1-D array; pandas.DataFrame: a table with an index and named columns.
  • See Lecture 2 for details.

Part 4: Python classes

11. OOP and encapsulation

  • A class = a custom data structure bundling data (attributes) with the functions (methods) that act on it.
  • Benefit: encapsulation — binding data and methods together makes it harder to apply them to the wrong object.
class MyClass:
    """This is my cool class."""
    def my_method(self, a, b):
        self.val = a + b     # store an instance attribute
        return a * b

inst = MyClass()             # create an instance with ()
a = inst.my_method(1, 2)     # a=2, inst.val=3

12. __init__ and instance attributes

class Point3D:
    def __init__(self, x, y, z):
        self.x = x; self.y = y; self.z = z

p = Point3D(1, 4, 7)
print(p.x, p.y, p.z)   # 1 4 7

13. Class attributes vs instance attributes (⚠️ common pitfall)

  • Class attributes (written in the class body, outside methods): shared by all instances.
  • Instance attributes (self.xxx): independent per instance.
class MyClass:
    mylist = []            # class attribute — shared by all instances!

inst1, inst2 = MyClass(), MyClass()
inst1.mylist.append(1); inst2.mylist.append(2)
print(inst1.mylist is inst2.mylist)   # True (the same list!)

Mutable types (like a list) as class attributes are especially dangerous — instances interfere with each other.

14. Inheritance

class MySubClass(MyBaseClass):
    '''MySubClass inherits from MyBaseClass'''
    # new methods here
  • Every class ultimately inherits from the base object (including int, list, …).
  • A subclass can override parent methods.
  • Inspect the base: Tree.__base__.
  • super() calls the parent's method without rewriting it entirely.
class Shrub(Tree):
    def __init__(self, species, age, height, fruit):
        super().__init__(species, age, height)   # call the parent __init__
        self.fruit = fruit

15. Properties: make a function feel like an attribute

class Temperature:
    def __init__(self, temp):
        self.celsius = temp

    @property
    def fahrenheit(self):
        return self.celsius * 9/5 + 32

    @fahrenheit.setter
    def fahrenheit(self, temp):
        self.celsius = (temp - 32) * 5/9

16. Magic (special) methods

Trigger Method
inst() __call__(self)
print(inst) __str__(self)
inst (interactive display) __repr__(self)
inst1 + inst2 __add__ (operator overloading)
  • Overloading rule: don't surprise people — + should add/append, - should subtract/remove.

17. __new__ and __del__ (advanced — skippable)

  • Creating an instance calls __new__ then __init__ (usually you only write __init__).
  • __del__ runs when the garbage collector considers the object no longer needed — use it for special cleanup.

Part 5: Classes and deep learning (PyTorch)

18. From a neuron to PyTorch

Base neuron (linear model: weighted sum + bias):

class Neuron:
    def __init__(self, weights, bias):
        self.weights = weights; self.bias = bias
    def forward(self, inputs):
        return sum(w*i for w,i in zip(self.weights, inputs)) + self.bias

Add activation functions via inheritance (ReLU / Sigmoid):

class ReLUNeuron(Neuron):
    def relu(self, x): return max(0, x)
    def forward(self, inputs):
        return self.relu(super().forward(inputs))   # parent computes linear, then activate

19. PyTorch's nn.Module

  • In PyTorch, everything "neural" inherits from torch.nn.Module, which manages parameters, device movement, save/load, and autograd.
  • Key points:
    • super().__init__() initialises the parent.
    • nn.Linear registers learnable parameters automatically.
    • forward defines the computation.
class CustomNeuron(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = nn.Linear(input_size, 1)
        self.relu = nn.ReLU()
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.relu(self.linear(x))

Multi-layer perceptron (MLP):

class TinyMLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, hidden_size, num_classes):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(input_size, hidden_size)
        self.act = nn.ReLU()
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(hidden_size, num_classes)
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.fc2(self.act(self.fc1(x)))

20. Key takeaways

  • Classes encapsulate data (attributes) and behaviour (methods).
  • Inheritance lets you define a blueprint once and specialise it in subclasses.
  • PyTorch uses this pattern everywhere: models and layers inherit from nn.Module, providing parameter handling, device management, and autograd integration.
  • Understanding classes and inheritance makes DL frameworks more transparent and your own models easier to design, debug, and extend.

Common pitfalls ⚠️

  1. Mutable types (list/dict/set) as class attributes are shared across instances — put them in __init__ instead.
  2. Generators can be iterated only once.
  3. a = b for a mutable object is a shallow binding (same object) — mutating a affects b.
  4. Dict keys must be immutable and hashable.
  5. Use super() to extend (rather than fully replace) parent logic in a subclass.

item.title: Marcov_chain_prediction_algorithm
item.description:
What is a Markov Chain?

A Markov Chain is a mathematical model describing transitions between states based on probabilities. Its defining property is that the future state depends only on the current state, not on past states.

Markov Property

The Markov Property is expressed mathematically as:

$$ P(X_{t+1} = s_j | X_t = s_i, X_{t-1}, …, X_0) = P(X_{t+1} = s_j | X_t = s_i) $$

State Transition Probability Matrix

The state transitions in a Markov Chain are described by a state transition probability matrix, ( P ):

$$ P = \begin{bmatrix} 0.7 & 0.2 & 0.1 \ 0.3 & 0.4 & 0.3 \ 0.2 & 0.3 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix} $$

Each entry ( P(s_j|s_i) ) represents the probability of transitioning from state ( s_i ) to state ( s_j ). The rows of the matrix must sum to 1.

Visual Representation

Initial State Distribution

The initial state distribution is represented as a vector ( \pi ). For example:

$$ \pi^{(0)} = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0] $$

This means the system starts entirely in state ( s_1 ) (eating out).

Prediction Formula

To predict the state distribution at the next time step, use the formula:

$$ \pi^{(t+1)} = \pi^{(t)} \cdot P $$

Repeat this process iteratively to predict the distribution over multiple steps.

Practical Example: Deciding Daily Activities

Imagine you’re deciding what to do tomorrow:

  1. Eat out (( s_1 )).
  2. Go for a walk (( s_2 )).
  3. Grab coffee (( s_3 )).

Based on your habits:

  • If you eat out today, there’s a 70% chance you’ll eat out again tomorrow, 20% chance for a walk, and 10% chance for coffee.
  • Similar transition probabilities apply for other states.

The state transition matrix ( P ) and initial state distribution ( \pi ) are as shown earlier. Let’s predict your activity distribution over the next 10 days.

Python Implementation

import numpy as np

# Define the state transition matrix
P = np.array([
    [0.7, 0.2, 0.1],
    [0.3, 0.4, 0.3],
    [0.2, 0.3, 0.5]
])

# Define the initial state (starting with eating out)
initial_state = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 0.0])

# Function to predict future states
def predict_markov_chain(P, initial_state, steps):
    state = initial_state
    predictions = []
    for step in range(steps):
        state = np.dot(state, P)
        predictions.append(state)
        print(f"Step {step + 1}: {state}")
    return predictions

# Run the prediction for 10 steps
steps = 10
predicted_states = predict_markov_chain(P, initial_state, steps)
print("Predicted State Distribution After 10 Steps:", predicted_states[-1])

Example Output

Running the above code produces the following output:

Step 2: [0.58 0.28 0.14]
Step 3: [0.494 0.318 0.188]
...
Step 10: [0.4 0.3 0.3]

By the 10th day, the probabilities stabilize at ( [0.4, 0.3, 0.3] ), indicating equal chances for eating out, walking, or grabbing coffee.

Conclusion

Markov Chains are versatile and easy to implement. Whether predicting daily decisions, modeling weather patterns, or generating text, they provide a powerful framework for understanding probabilistic systems.

Supplementary code for the Build a Large Language Model From Scratch book by Sebastian Raschka


Code repository: https://github.com/rasbt/LLMs-from-scratch

Chapter 2: Working with Text

Packages that are being used in this notebook:

  • This chapter covers data preparation and sampling to get input data “ready” for the LLM

2.1 Understanding word embeddings

  • No code in this section

  • There are many forms of embeddings; we focus on text embeddings in this book

  • LLMs work with embeddings in high-dimensional spaces (i.e., thousands of dimensions)

  • Since we can’t visualize such high-dimensional spaces (we humans think in 1, 2, or 3 dimensions), the figure below illustrates a 2-dimensional embedding space

2.2 Tokenizing text

  • In this section, we tokenize text, which means breaking text into smaller units, such as individual words and punctuation characters

  • Load raw text we want to work with

  • The Verdict by Edith Wharton is a public domain short story

  • (If you encounter an ssl.SSLCertVerificationError when executing the previous code cell, it might be due to using an outdated Python version; you can find more information here on GitHub)

  • The goal is to tokenize and embed this text for an LLM

  • Let’s develop a simple tokenizer based on some simple sample text that we can then later apply to the text above

  • The following regular expression will split on whitespaces

  • We don’t only want to split on whitespaces but also commas and periods, so let’s modify the regular expression to do that as well

  • As we can see, this creates empty strings, let’s remove them

  • This looks pretty good, but let’s also handle other types of punctuation, such as periods, question marks, and so on

  • This is pretty good, and we are now ready to apply this tokenization to the raw text

  • Let’s calculate the total number of tokens

2.3 Converting tokens into token IDs

  • Next, we convert the text tokens into token IDs that we can process via embedding layers later

  • From these tokens, we can now build a vocabulary that consists of all the unique tokens

  • Below are the first 50 entries in this vocabulary:

  • Below, we illustrate the tokenization of a short sample text using a small vocabulary:

  • Putting it now all together into a tokenizer class

  • The encode function turns text into token IDs

  • The decode function turns token IDs back into text

  • We can use the tokenizer to encode (that is, tokenize) texts into integers

  • These integers can then be embedded (later) as input of/for the LLM

  • We can decode the integers back into text

2.4 Adding special context tokens

  • It’s useful to add some “special” tokens for unknown words and to denote the end of a text

  • Some tokenizers use special tokens to help the LLM with additional context

  • Some of these special tokens are

    • [BOS] (beginning of sequence) marks the beginning of text

    • [EOS] (end of sequence) marks where the text ends (this is usually used to concatenate multiple unrelated texts, e.g., two different Wikipedia articles or two different books, and so on)

    • [PAD] (padding) if we train LLMs with a batch size greater than 1 (we may include multiple texts with different lengths; with the padding token we pad the shorter texts to the longest length so that all texts have an equal length)

  • [UNK] to represent words that are not included in the vocabulary

  • Note that GPT-2 does not need any of these tokens mentioned above but only uses an <|endoftext|> token to reduce complexity

  • The <|endoftext|> is analogous to the [EOS] token mentioned above

  • GPT also uses the <|endoftext|> for padding (since we typically use a mask when training on batched inputs, we would not attend padded tokens anyways, so it does not matter what these tokens are)

  • GPT-2 does not use an <UNK> token for out-of-vocabulary words; instead, GPT-2 uses a byte-pair encoding (BPE) tokenizer, which breaks down words into subword units which we will discuss in a later section

  • We use the <|endoftext|> tokens between two independent sources of text:

  • Let’s see what happens if we tokenize the following text:

  • The above produces an error because the word “Hello” is not contained in the vocabulary

  • To deal with such cases, we can add special tokens like "<|unk|>" to the vocabulary to represent unknown words

  • Since we are already extending the vocabulary, let’s add another token called "<|endoftext|>" which is used in GPT-2 training to denote the end of a text (and it’s also used between concatenated text, like if our training datasets consists of multiple articles, books, etc.)

  • We also need to adjust the tokenizer accordingly so that it knows when and how to use the new <unk> token Let’s try to tokenize text with the modified tokenizer:

2.5 BytePair encoding

  • GPT-2 used BytePair encoding (BPE) as its tokenizer

  • it allows the model to break down words that aren’t in its predefined vocabulary into smaller subword units or even individual characters, enabling it to handle out-of-vocabulary words

  • For instance, if GPT-2’s vocabulary doesn’t have the word “unfamiliarword,” it might tokenize it as [“unfam”, “iliar”, “word”] or some other subword breakdown, depending on its trained BPE merges

  • The original BPE tokenizer can be found here: https://github.com/openai/gpt-2/blob/master/src/encoder.py

  • In this chapter, we are using the BPE tokenizer from OpenAI’s open-source tiktoken library, which implements its core algorithms in Rust to improve computational performance

  • I created a notebook in the ./bytepair_encoder that compares these two implementations side-by-side (tiktoken was about 5x faster on the sample text)

  • BPE tokenizers break down unknown words into subwords and individual characters:

2.6 Data sampling with a sliding window

  • We train LLMs to generate one word at a time, so we want to prepare the training data accordingly where the next word in a sequence represents the target to predict:

  • For each text chunk, we want the inputs and targets

  • Since we want the model to predict the next word, the targets are the inputs shifted by one position to the right

  • One by one, the prediction would look like as follows:

  • We will take care of the next-word prediction in a later chapter after we covered the attention mechanism

  • For now, we implement a simple data loader that iterates over the input dataset and returns the inputs and targets shifted by one

  • Install and import PyTorch (see Appendix A for installation tips)

  • We use a sliding window approach, changing the position by +1:

- Create dataset and dataloader that extract chunks from the input text dataset - Let's test the dataloader with a batch size of 1 for an LLM with a context size of 4: - An example using stride equal to the context length (here: 4) as shown below: - We can also create batched outputs
  • Note that we increase the stride here so that we don’t have overlaps between the batches, since more overlap could lead to increased overfitting

2.7 Creating token embeddings

  • The data is already almost ready for an LLM

  • But lastly let us embed the tokens in a continuous vector representation using an embedding layer

  • Usually, these embedding layers are part of the LLM itself and are updated (trained) during model training

  • Suppose we have the following four input examples with input ids 2, 3, 5, and 1 (after tokenization):

  • For the sake of simplicity, suppose we have a small vocabulary of only 6 words and we want to create embeddings of size 3:

  • This would result in a 6x3 weight matrix:

  • For those who are familiar with one-hot encoding, the embedding layer approach above is essentially just a more efficient way of implementing one-hot encoding followed by matrix multiplication in a fully-connected layer, which is described in the supplementary code in ./embedding_vs_matmul

  • Because the embedding layer is just a more efficient implementation that is equivalent to the one-hot encoding and matrix-multiplication approach it can be seen as a neural network layer that can be optimized via backpropagation

  • To convert a token with id 3 into a 3-dimensional vector, we do the following:

  • Note that the above is the 4th row in the embedding_layer weight matrix

  • To embed all four input_ids values above, we do

  • An embedding layer is essentially a look-up operation:

  • You may be interested in the bonus content comparing embedding layers with regular linear layers: ../03_bonus_embedding-vs-matmul

2.8 Encoding word positions

  • Embedding layer convert IDs into identical vector representations regardless of where they are located in the input sequence:

  • Positional embeddings are combined with the token embedding vector to form the input embeddings for a large language model:

  • The BytePair encoder has a vocabulary size of 50,257:

  • Suppose we want to encode the input tokens into a 256-dimensional vector representation:

  • If we sample data from the dataloader, we embed the tokens in each batch into a 256-dimensional vector

  • If we have a batch size of 8 with 4 tokens each, this results in a 8 x 4 x 256 tensor:

  • GPT-2 uses absolute position embeddings, so we just create another embedding layer:

  • To create the input embeddings used in an LLM, we simply add the token and the positional embeddings:

  • In the initial phase of the input processing workflow, the input text is segmented into separate tokens

  • Following this segmentation, these tokens are transformed into token IDs based on a predefined vocabulary:

item.title: Math Typesetting
item.description:
Mathematical notation in a Hugo project can be enabled by using third party JavaScript libraries.

In this example we will be using KaTeX

  • Create a partial under /layouts/partials/math.html
  • Within this partial reference the Auto-render Extension or host these scripts locally.
  • Include the partial in your templates like so:
1
2
3

{{ if or .Params.math .Site.Params.math }}
{{ partial "math.html" . }}
{{ end }}
  • To enable KaTeX globally set the parameter math to true in a project’s configuration
  • To enable KaTeX on a per page basis include the parameter math: true in content files

Note: Use the online reference of Supported TeX Functions

Examples

Inline math: $\varphi = \dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}= 1.6180339887…$

Block math: $$ \varphi = 1+\frac{1} {1+\frac{1} {1+\frac{1} {1+\cdots} } } $$

item.title: About
item.description:
Written in Go, Hugo is an open source static site generator available under the Apache License 2.0. Hugo supports TOML, YAML and JSON data file types, Markdown and HTML content files and uses shortcodes to add rich content. Other notable features are taxonomies, multilingual mode, image processing, custom output formats, HTML/CSS/JS minification and support for Sass SCSS workflows.

Hugo makes use of a variety of open source projects including:

  • https://github.com/yuin/goldmark
  • https://github.com/alecthomas/chroma
  • https://github.com/muesli/smartcrop
  • https://github.com/spf13/cobra
  • https://github.com/spf13/viper

Hugo is ideal for blogs, corporate websites, creative portfolios, online magazines, single page applications or even a website with thousands of pages.

Hugo is for people who want to hand code their own website without worrying about setting up complicated runtimes, dependencies and databases.

Websites built with Hugo are extremely fast, secure and can be deployed anywhere including, AWS, GitHub Pages, Heroku, Netlify and any other hosting provider.

Learn more and contribute on GitHub.
